summary: A short note from the UCSB Computer Research Lab saying its 360-75 got a new production network interface, replacing the older one, which began operation on May 1, 1972. It resembles the units used at NASA Ames and USC. Users are asked to report any trouble that might relate to it.

plainLanguage.summary: A school replaced the plug that connects its big computer to the network and asks everyone to tell them if anything seems to work strangely.

subtitle: UCSB upgraded its computer's connection to the ARPANET

tldr.problem: UCSB's 360-75 mainframe's original interface to the ARPANET had been in use and needed replacement with a production unit.
tldr.mechanism: On May 1, 1972, UCSB replaced its IMP interface with a new production unit similar to those already deployed at NASA Ames and USC, putting the new hardware into operation that same day.
tldr.outcome: The ARPANET gained a more reliable connection at UCSB. The new interface was a standard production model proven at other sites.

today: RFC 335 is a brief operational notice documenting a network equipment upgrade. It reflects the collaborative nature of early ARPANET operations, where sites coordinated infrastructure changes and shared feedback about reliability.

sections.title: UCSB's Network Interface Upgrade
sections.content: On May 1, 1972, the UCSB Computer Research Lab announced that it had replaced the network interface on its IBM System/360-75 mainframe. The old interface was replaced with a production unit, similar to those already installed and operating at NASA Ames and USC.
sections.plainLanguage: UCSB got a new box to connect its computer to the network, just like the ones NASA and USC were using.

sections.title: Rollout and Support
sections.content: The new interface unit went into operation on May 1, 1972. As a precautionary measure, Roland F. Bryan and the UCSB Computer Research Lab asked network users to report any difficulties they encountered while operating with UCSB that might be related to the new interface. This invitation for feedback ensured that any problems could be quickly identified and addressed.
sections.plainLanguage: The new connection started working right away, and UCSB asked people to say if anything went wrong so they could fix it.

sections.title: Production Hardware Standards
sections.content: The new interface was a production unit, not an experimental one, and was similar to units already deployed and proven at two other major ARPANET sites: NASA Ames and the University of Southern California (USC). Using standardized, tested hardware from the same production line meant that UCSB could benefit from the operational experience and fixes from these other sites.
sections.plainLanguage: The new equipment was the same kind that worked well at other schools, so UCSB knew it was good.
